hook: The first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and the only person to win in two sciences.

pages.x: Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw in 1867, when Poland was ruled by Russia and women could not go to university. She studied at the "Flying University", whose classes moved from house to house in secret.

She worked for years as a governess to pay for her sister's studies, then followed her to Paris in 1891. She lived in an attic so cold that she slept under all her clothes, and once fainted from hunger. She came first in her class in physics.
In 1894 she met the physicist Pierre Curie. They married the next year; she wore a dark blue dress she could use in the laboratory, and they went on honeymoon by bicycle.

She found that the rays given off by uranium come from inside its atoms, and named this radioactivity. In 1898, working in a leaky shed, she and Pierre discovered two new elements: polonium, named after Poland, and radium.
pages.fx: It showed that atoms are not solid and unchanging, opening the way to nuclear physics. Radiation was soon used to treat cancer.

pages.x: In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, the first woman ever to win a Nobel. In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own. She is still the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences.
In 1906 Pierre was knocked down and killed by a horse-drawn wagon in a Paris street. She took over his post, and became the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne.
In the First World War she set up X-ray vans, nicknamed "little Curies", drove them to the front herself, and trained women to run them. More than a million wounded soldiers were X-rayed.

She carried radium in her pockets and kept it in her desk, and liked its soft glow in the dark. She died in 1934 of an illness caused by radiation. Her notebooks are still so radioactive that they are kept in lead boxes.
Curie discovered the secrets of radioactivity and two new elements, opened the way to nuclear physics and cancer treatment, and showed the world what women scientists could do.
pts: First woman to win a Nobel Prize
The only person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences
